title: Making accessibility review part of delivery
provenance: Authored fictional script; no real customer recording

segments.speaker: Synthetic narrator
segments.text: Welcome to this synthetic Morrow field session, Making accessibility review part of delivery. This presentation is an authored example for testing an editorial workflow. The company, project situations, and participants are fictional. Our working proposition is simple: Accessibility improves when real tasks are tested throughout delivery, not only at release. We will examine six decisions, not a universal formula. Each example is a scenario, and any number I mention belongs to that scenario unless I explicitly say otherwise. The aim is to make an audience more precise about what it can conclude from source material. A content editor should be able to return to this recording, read the complete surrounding passage, and decide whether a headline preserves its meaning. We will also correct an earlier statement when the evidence changes. That correction is part of the story, not an embarrassment to remove.

segments.speaker: Synthetic narrator
segments.text: A participant asks: What changed your view of task selection, and which observation is strongest? Let me start with a concrete observation. In digital accessibility, a home page audit can miss the workflow people actually need. That sounds ordinary, but it changes what a team should inspect before choosing a remedy. For instance, a fictional buyer could browse pricing but could not finish the upload form by keyboard. This is a fictional situation, not a customer result. The useful detail is the sequence: someone made an assumption, the work proceeded, and a later fact exposed the gap. If we reduce the whole episode to an upbeat slogan, we lose the decision the team actually faced. The first question should therefore be what is observable in the source, what remains inferred, and who can verify the missing part. That distinction matters when this recording becomes a newsletter or a short clip.

segments.speaker: Synthetic narrator
segments.text: Here is the practical move I would make: choose critical journeys for repeated checks. I would write that action where the people doing the work can see it, attach an owner, and define what evidence would change our mind. The point is not to add a ritual. The point is to make a choice that another person can inspect next week. In the fictional example, I would ask the responsible team to show the original record and one counterexample before declaring the issue solved. A presentation can make that step sound neat, while daily work is usually messier. We should preserve that messiness in a source note. If an editor selects a sentence from here, the claim needs this surrounding explanation, because the recommendation is conditional and depends on the observed situation.

segments.text: A follow-up question is what could make this recommendation wrong. My answer is: an automated scan covers only a subset of barriers.
